appraisal_events.evidence: Le chasseur louche monopolise la montée en ascenseur pour vanter la fortune de sa sœur et de son frère, flatte le narrateur (« Si tout le monde avait aussi bon cœur que vous il n’y aurait plus de malheureux ») puis lui reproche : « Mais je vous fais babiller (je n’avais pas dit une seule parole et je commençais à m’endormir en écoutant les siennes) ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator is locally reduced to a mute, drowsy captive audience for a servant's boastful vulgarity; the parenthesis he inserts turns the flattery and the accusation of chattiness against himself, so his rhetorical standing in the exchange is comically effaced rather than asserted.

appraisal_events.evidence: « moi l’étrange humain qui, en attendant que la mort le délivre, vis les volets clos, ne sais rien du monde, reste immobile comme un hibou » ; puis, au réveil : « Ma grand’mère n’a plus que quelques semaines à vivre, assure le docteur. » Il sonne, il pleure à l’idée que ce ne sera pas, comme autrefois, sa grand’mère, sa grand’mère mourante, mais un indifférent valet de chambre qui va venir.
appraisal_events.explanation: The sleep meditation culminates in an unironized self-diminishment: the narrator presents himself as a shuttered, owl-like invalid awaiting death, and the waking movement delivers grief over the grandmother's approaching death and her replacement by an indifferent servant.

status_effects.explanation: The passage's culminating movement leaves him weeping, disoriented, and stripped of consolation, with the grandmother's dying replaced by an indifferent valet.
In the elevator scene he says nothing at all, is talked at, flattered, and told he is the one babbling; he holds no rhetorical ground.

ambiguities: The satirical energy of the first paragraph is aimed chiefly at the unnamed « chasseur louche » and his family (the sister as « une grande dame » who fouls wardrobes, the brother's « prince indien », his own dream of the presidency). Because that figure is unnamed and absent from the reference sheet, he cannot be recorded, so E1 registers only the residual effect on the narrator; a scope that admitted him would make him the dominant target instead.

The waking sequence is narrated in a generalized third person (« le dormeur », « il sonne, il pleure »), so the grieving sleeper is formally impersonal; the surrounding first person (« ces réveils… qui étaient la plupart du temps les miens », « je peux en témoigner ») supports reading it as the narrator's own experience, which is how E2 is scored. Relatedly, « le docteur » is a bare form not resolvable between Cottard and du Boulbon, and is left unattached.
